# Get started on NuttX in QEMU (RISC-V)

<!-- type: how-to · level: 1 -->

**Needs first:** [Install](../start/install.md)

<!-- BEGIN GENERATED by scripts/gen-board-support.py: starter status -->
> **Status:** Verified in emulator (daily). From the board support registry: [`nros-board-nuttx-qemu`](../reference/boards/nuttx-riscv.md); [Board Support Levels](../reference/board-support-levels.md) explains the words.
<!-- END GENERATED starter status -->

This starter puts a talker on Apache NuttX, on QEMU's 32-bit RISC-V `virt`
machine (`rv32imac`), and shows its messages arriving in ROS 2. NuttX is a
POSIX-style RTOS, so the talker runs as an ordinary NuttX task, with NuttX's
own network stack on a virtio-net device. You need no NuttX checkout of your
own: `nros setup` fetches the kernel and its apps tree, and `nros run` links
your node into a bootable kernel. You write the talker in Rust or in C; pick
a tab and every tab on the page follows.

## What you need

- A Linux host with the [install](../start/install.md) done, so `nros` is on
  your `PATH`.
- ROS 2 Humble with `ros-humble-rmw-zenoh-cpp`. ROS 2 provides the zenoh
  router the board talks to, and the message definitions the build generates
  the talker's code from.
- Two host packages the NuttX kernel build uses, the Python venv module and
  `unzip`, which the provision step installs for you when you allow it.
- A `qemu-system-riscv32` from your distribution. The QEMU in nano-ros's
  store is built for Arm and 64-bit RISC-V only, so this board takes yours.
  On Debian or Ubuntu it is in `qemu-system-misc`.

No board, no cable: QEMU's user-mode network carries the guest's ethernet to
your machine, with no TAP device to create. WiFi is deferred to the Zephyr
4.4 line, so no starter opens over WiFi yet.

## Provision

```bash probe=30
nros setup rv-virt-nuttx --rmw zenoh --sudo
sudo apt-get install -y qemu-system-misc
```

The first line fetches the RISC-V cross-compiler and the NuttX kernel and apps
sources into a shared store under `~/.nros`. Before it downloads anything it
names the host packages that are missing, and `--sudo` lets it run the one
install command it composed for your package manager. Leave `--sudo` off and
it only prints that command. The second line installs the emulator. Neither
installs a router: the router is ROS's `rmw_zenohd`.

## Scaffold the project

`QEMU_SYSTEM_RISCV32` names the emulator `nros run` boots the board with, so
set it in the shell you build and run from:

<!-- tabs -->

### Rust

```bash probe=40
export QEMU_SYSTEM_RISCV32="$(command -v qemu-system-riscv32)"
nros new nx_ws --board rv-virt-nuttx --template talker --lang rust
cd nx_ws
```

### C

```bash probe=40
export QEMU_SYSTEM_RISCV32="$(command -v qemu-system-riscv32)"
nros new nx_ws --board rv-virt-nuttx --template talker --lang c
cd nx_ws
```

<!-- /tabs -->

That wrote a workspace with two packages: `src/nx_node/`, the talker, a
library with no `main()` that names no board, and `src/nx_node_bringup/`,
which says what the talker runs on. The NuttX task that runs your node is
generated from the bringup when you build. A Rust talker builds for the
board's `riscv32imac-unknown-nuttx-elf` target, which the build compiles the
Rust standard library for itself.

## Run it in QEMU

The guest sits on QEMU's user-mode network at `10.0.2.15`, and dials the
router through the gateway `10.0.2.2`, which is your host, on port 7447.
Start the router first, in its own terminal, listening on every interface so
the guest's connection arrives:

<!-- removed when the board descriptor states its default locator -->
```bash probe=50 probe-run=60 probe-keep
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
ZENOH_CONFIG_OVERRIDE='listen/endpoints=["tcp/0.0.0.0:7447"];scouting/multicast/enabled=false' \
    ros2 run rmw_zenoh_cpp rmw_zenohd
```

```text probe-expect=50
Started Zenoh router with id
```

Then, back in the workspace terminal, source ROS 2 and build and run the
talker. This first run records the ROS 2 prefix in the workspace, so later
runs of it need no sourced shell:

```bash probe=60 probe-run=1500
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
nros run nx_node --expect 'Publishing:'
```

```text probe-expect=60
Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
nros run: matched after
```

`nros run` builds the kernel with your node linked in (the first build
configures NuttX from the board's defconfig and takes several minutes; later
builds take seconds), then boots it with the `qemu-system-riscv32` that
`QEMU_SYSTEM_RISCV32` names. The image starts its application itself, so
what you see is the talker on the NuttX console. With `--expect` it stops
QEMU and exits 0 at the first console line containing that text, and exits 1
if the board stops first. The router keeps running.

Without `--expect` it keeps running until you press Ctrl-C, which stops QEMU:

```bash probe=65 probe-run=120 probe-keep
nros run nx_node
```

```text probe-expect=65
Publishing: 'Hello World: 1'
Publishing: 'Hello World: 2'
```

## See it in ROS 2

Leave the router and `nros run` going. In a third terminal:

```bash probe=70 probe-run=120
source /opt/ros/humble/setup.bash
export RMW_IMPLEMENTATION=rmw_zenoh_cpp
ros2 topic echo /chatter std_msgs/msg/String --qos-reliability best_effort
```

```text probe-expect=70
data: 'Hello World:
```

The talker publishes best-effort, and `ros2 topic echo` defaults to reliable,
which receives nothing from it. That is why the command asks for best-effort.

## If it doesn't work

- **`nros run` asks `nros locate tool qemu-system-riscv32`, or names no
  emulator:** this shell has no `QEMU_SYSTEM_RISCV32`. Run the `export` line
  again, after installing `qemu-system-misc`.
- **No `Publishing:` line within a minute of boot:** the talker did not reach
  the router. Check that the router listens on `0.0.0.0:7447`: one on
  `127.0.0.1` is out of the guest's reach.
- **`nros setup` stops and names `python3-venv` or `unzip`:** you left
  `--sudo` off. Run the command it printed.
- **Everything else:** [Troubleshooting - First 10 Minutes](../reference/troubleshooting-index.md).
